# Secrets Humans Can Transcribe

Two moments in the life of a FOKS account require a secret to pass through a
person rather than a wire. The first is the *recovery kit*: a phrase printed
at signup and stored somewhere safe, used only when every device is lost.
The second is the *pairing code*: a phrase displayed on an existing device
and typed into a new one to enrol it. A third, optional, mechanism lets a
person choose a passphrase for logging in where no device key is available.

Each of these has different security requirements and gets a different
treatment. The recovery kit protects data at rest indefinitely and needs
full-strength entropy. The pairing code is single-use and lives for five
minutes, so it can be shorter. The passphrase is chosen by a human and is
weak by construction, so it must be stretched. This chapter covers the
encoding that the first two share, then each mechanism in turn.

## Encoding bits as words and numbers

Hexadecimal is an unforgiving way to transcribe a secret: 52 characters
from an alphabet where `0`/`O` and `1`/`l` look alike, with no structure to
help a reader keep their place. Word lists are better. The BIP-39 list used
by cryptocurrency wallets has 2048 English words chosen so that the first
four letters are unique and visually similar words are excluded; each word
carries 11 bits. A 26-byte secret would need 19 words.

FOKS uses a *mixed-radix* encoding instead, called HESP (human-exact secret
phrase). The secret is treated as one large integer and expanded into
digits of alternating radix: a base-2048 digit (a word), then a base-$2^k$
digit (a decimal number), and so on. Mixed-radix conversion is the classic
algorithm from Knuth's treatment of radix conversion: repeatedly take the
value modulo the current radix, emit that digit, divide, and move to the
next radix. FOKS's implementation works on the byte array directly,
extracting the low 11 or $k$ bits and shifting the whole array right.

The two encodings in use are:

| | Recovery kit | Pairing code |
|---|---|---|
| Secret size | 26 bytes | 16 bytes |
| Tokens | 17: 9 words + 8 numbers | 13: 7 words + 6 numbers |
| Bits per word | 11 | 11 |
| Bits per number | 13 (range 0–8191) | 8 (range 0–255) |
| Entropy | 9 × 11 + 8 × 13 = 203 bits | 7 × 11 + 6 × 8 = 125 bits |
| Unused high bits | 5 (mask `0x07` on byte 0) | 3 (mask `0x1f` on byte 0) |

The phrase alternates word, number, word, number, ..., word. The first token
comes from the lowest bits of the secret. As a concrete example from the
test suite, the 16-byte pairing secret consisting of sixteen `0x01` bytes
encodes as

```
cage 32 advice 4 letter 128 avoid 16 acoustic 2 doctor 64 amount
```

The repository guide gives three reasons for mixing numbers into the
phrase. The alternating shapes give a transcription cadence that makes
skipped or duplicated tokens easy to notice. A large share of the entropy
(104 of 203 bits in the recovery kit) is numeric, so a language model or
dictionary attack on the word positions alone gains little. And the phrase
needs no checksum, for a reason explained next.

### Exactness

BIP-39 appends a checksum: the last word's low bits are a hash of the
entropy, so a mistyped phrase is usually detected. HESP has no checksum.
Instead the parser is strict. Every word must be found by binary search in
the 2048-entry list; every number must parse and lie within its range;
after all tokens are pushed back, the unused high bits of byte 0 must be
zero, and any arithmetic overflow during reconstruction is an error. The
consequence is that every phrase corresponds to exactly one secret and
every secret to exactly one phrase, a property the test suite checks by
round-tripping random secrets and by comparing against a fixture produced by
the Go implementation. A typo that produces a valid word or in-range number
is *not* detected at parse time; it is detected when the resulting key fails
to open anything. For the pairing code, which is confirmed interactively
within seconds, that is acceptable. For the recovery kit, such a typo is
discovered only at recovery time, when the reconstructed key fails to open
the parcel addressed to the real backup key.

## The recovery kit

The 26-byte recovery secret is not used as a key directly. It is hashed
under a type ID to produce a standard 32-byte seed:

```
seed = SHA-512/256( BE64(BACKUP_SEED_TYPE_ID) ‖ bin8(secret26) )
```

where `bin8(...)` is the canonical two-byte binary header followed by the 26
bytes. The code builds this 28-byte buffer by hand in zeroizing storage
rather than calling the generic encoder, so the secret never lands in an
ordinary heap allocation. From the seed, the full key suite of
[Chapter 3](03-key-hierarchy.qmd) follows, with entity type 16 (backup key).
The first word and number of the phrase double as the backup key's public
device name, so a user can tell which kit corresponds to which enrolled key.

The repository's introduction and guide both say the recovery kit is
"stretched via Argon2id (64 MiB memory, 3 iterations)". The code does not
do this: the recovery seed is only typed-hashed as above. Argon2id with
those parameters is applied to user *passphrases* (below). The code is right
and the documentation is loose. With 203 bits of entropy, stretching would
add nothing; Argon2id exists to slow down guessing, and nobody guesses a
203-bit value.

### Enrolled as a device

The backup key is not a special object on the server. It is enrolled as a
*device* of the chosen role, with its own entity ID and HEPK, through the
same provisioning link an ordinary device uses. This has a consequence that
matters for a printed document: every later PUK rotation
([Chapter 5](05-generations.qmd)) boxes the new generation to the backup
key's HEPK exactly as it does to any other device. A kit printed at signup
stays valid across any number of rotations and device changes. Nothing on
paper ever needs updating.

### Recovery

When all devices are lost, the user types the phrase on a new machine. The
client reconstructs the backup seed and its suite, authenticates to the
server over mutual TLS with the backup key's Ed25519 key (wrapped in
PKCS#8 like any device key), fetches the latest PUK parcel addressed to the
backup key, opens it, and then acts as the *existing* device in an ordinary
provisioning: it builds a link enrolling the new machine's freshly generated
device key, boxes the current PUK to the new device's HEPK, countersigns,
and submits. The backup key never becomes the daily device; it is the
bootstrap that authorises one.

## The pairing code and KEX

Enrolling a second device must not move the user's seeds through the server
in a form the server can read, and neither device has any prior trust
relationship with the other. The pairing code supplies the shared secret
that bootstraps a private channel through the server, which acts only as a
relay.

From the 16-byte pairing secret two keys are derived, both by typed HMAC:

```
session_id    = HMAC-SHA-512/256( secret, BE64(KEX_KEY_DERIVATION_TYPE_ID) ‖ encode([0, {}]) )
secretbox_key = HMAC-SHA-512/256( secret, BE64(KEX_KEY_DERIVATION_TYPE_ID) ‖ encode([1, {}]) )
```

The session ID is public: the relay uses it to match senders and receivers.
The secret-box key never leaves the two devices.

### The protocol

The *provisioner* is the existing device (which must hold the owner role);
the *provisionee* is the new one. Every arrow below is one relay message.

```
 Provisioner (existing)                 Relay                  Provisionee (new)
 ───────────────────────                ─────                  ─────────────────
 generate secret, show phrase
 seq 0: Start ─────────────────────────>  ·
                                          ·   <── user types phrase; derive keys
                                          ·      generate new device seed
                                          ·  <──────────── seq 0: Hello {entity, hepk, name}
 verify Hello; build provisioning link
 naming the new device + HEPK fingerprint;
 box current PUK to new HEPK
 seq 1: PleaseSign {unsigned link, ppe?, token} ──>  ·
                                          ·      check link names *my* device,
                                          ·      *my* HEPK fingerprint, role ≠ None,
                                          ·      right host and user; sign first
                                          ·  <──────────── seq 1: OkSigned {signature}
 verify signature; countersign second;
 submit through the durable write path;
 wait until the chain shows the device
 seq 2: Done ──────────────────────────>  ·
                                          ·      fetch certificate chain; done
```

Every packet on the relay is a `KexWrapperMessage { session_id, sender,
sequence, payload }`, where `payload` is

```
XSalsa20-Poly1305( secretbox_key,
                   nonce = BE64(KEX_CLEARTEXT_TYPE_ID) ‖ 16 random bytes,
                   KexCleartext { session_id, sender, sequence, message } )
```

The cleartext repeats the session ID, sender and sequence number that
appear on the outside of the wrapper, and the receiver checks that they
match. A relay that re-attributes a packet to a different sender, reorders
by sequence number, or reflects a device's own packet back to it is
detected. Each wrapper is additionally signed with the sending device's
Ed25519 key. The relay verifies that signature, and that the sender is a
device entity, before queueing the packet, and it keeps only the first packet
for each (session, sender, sequence) slot. Any device key satisfies the relay,
so the signature attributes a packet to a key rather than excluding
strangers; a packet from a party that does not know the secret-box key simply
fails to open and is discarded by the receiver.

The provisionee's checks on the `PleaseSign` link are the heart of the
protocol. It decodes the proposed chain link and requires that it names
exactly one device change, that the entity is its own new device ID, that
the HEPK fingerprint is the fingerprint of its own HEPK, that the role is
not None, and that the host and (if known) user are the expected ones. Only
then does it sign. The provisioner, in turn, verifies the provisionee's
signature before adding its own. The link ends up with two stacked
signatures, new device first, existing owner second, which is the order the
server and every later verifier replays.

The whole exchange has a five-minute budget shared across all receives, and
each blocking receive at the relay is sliced into 30-second polls so that a
dropped connection does not tie up server resources for the full wait.

### Why 125 bits is enough here

The pairing secret is single-use and short-lived, the relay sees only
ciphertext, and an attacker must guess the secret *online*, before the two
devices finish, in order to inject a `Hello` of their own. Against that
threat, 125 bits is far beyond reach. The recovery kit protects data at rest
against an attacker with unlimited time and a copy of the ciphertexts, which
is why it gets 203 bits.

## Passphrase-protected encryption

Some deployments want a password login: a browser session, or a first
device with no other credential. Human-chosen passwords are weak, so two
things are required. The password must be stretched with a memory-hard
function to make offline guessing expensive. And because passwords change,
a *history* of the keys derived from them must be kept so that data sealed
under an old password remains reachable after a change.

### Stretching with Argon2id

Argon2id (RFC 9106) is the password-hashing function recommended for new
designs. It is *memory-hard*: computing it requires a configurable amount of
memory as well as time, which reduces the advantage that GPUs and custom
hardware have over ordinary processors for functions that need only
arithmetic. FOKS's production parameters are:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Algorithm | Argon2id, version 0x13 |
| Memory | 64 MiB (65 536 KiB) |
| Iterations | 3 |
| Parallelism (lanes) | 2 |
| Salt | 16 random bytes; an all-zero salt is rejected |
| Output | 64 bytes |

A second parameter set (512 KiB, 1 iteration, 1 lane) exists for
deterministic unit tests and is refused unless the caller explicitly opts
in. A test pins the production output to the Go implementation's
`argon2.IDKey(raw, salt, 3, 64*1024, 2, 64)`.

The 64-byte output is split. Bytes 0–31 become a `SecretSeed` from which a
full device-style key suite is derived with entity type 17 (passphrase
key); bytes 32–63 are reserved as a local box key, which the Rust code
derives but does not currently use. The passphrase key is therefore a
recipient like any other, with an Ed25519 verify key and an HEPK.

### The key history

Each passphrase *generation* has a random 32-byte wrapping key, called an
SKMWK in the code (secret key material wrapping key). The list of all of
them, tagged with the user and host, is encrypted under a fresh random
*session key* in a typed secretbox. That session key is then boxed twice:

- a **passphrase box**: a hybrid box ([Chapter 4](04-hybrid-encryption.qmd))
  from an ephemeral sender to the passphrase-derived HEPK, carrying the
  generation and the session key;
- a **PUK box**: a typed secretbox under `derive_key(owner_puk, 2)`,
  carrying the generation, the session key and the passphrase public key,
  with the owner PUK's generation recorded beside it.

Three operations fall out of this structure. A password change stretches
the new password, appends a new wrapping key to the list, and re-seals
everything; old wrapping keys are kept, so anything sealed under them still
opens. A PUK rotation can re-seal the whole parcel through the PUK box
*without the plaintext password*, because the owner PUK opens the session
key. And a login decrypts the passphrase box, recovers the current wrapping
key, and signs the server's registration challenge with the passphrase
key's Ed25519 key. The in-memory keyring zeroizes its keys on drop.

## Where to look

- `foks-crypto` (`backup.rs`): `BackupKey`, `RecoveryPhrase`, the
  `push_bits`/`take_low_bits` radix conversion, `derived_seed`,
  `device_name`.
- `foks-crypto` (`kex.rs`): `KexSecret`, `KexKeys`, `sign_kex_wrapper`,
  `countersign_software_kex_provision_link`,
  `finish_software_kex_provision_link`, `require_kex_device_binding`.
- `foks-crypto` (`passphrase.rs`): `stretch`, `StretchVersion`,
  `build_update`, `change_passphrase_with_puk`, `rotate_passphrase_for_puk`,
  `PassphraseKeyring`.
- `foks-proto` (`kex.rs`): `KexMessage`, `KexWrapperMessage`,
  `KexCleartext`.
- `foks-client` (`kex.rs`, `recovery.rs`, `passphrase.rs`): the
  provisioner and provisionee state machines, backup-key enrolment and
  recovery, passphrase login.

## Further reading

- M. Palatinus, P. Rusnak, A. Voisine, S. Bowe, *BIP-39: Mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys*, Bitcoin Improvement Proposals, 2013, https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039.mediawiki
- D. E. Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 2: Seminumerical Algorithms*, 3rd edition, section 4.4 (Radix Conversion), Addison-Wesley, 1997
- A. Biryukov, D. Dinu, D. Khovratovich, S. Josefsson, *Argon2 Memory-Hard Function for Password Hashing and Proof-of-Work Applications*, RFC 9106, IETF, 2021, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9106
- C. Percival, *Stronger Key Derivation via Sequential Memory-Hard Functions*, BSDCan, 2009, https://www.tarsnap.com/scrypt/scrypt.pdf
- OWASP Foundation, *Password Storage Cheat Sheet*, https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html
